title: Matrix Cells in Distance Order
summary: Given the integers row, cols, rCenter, and cCenter, list the coordinates of all cells in a rows x cols matrix, sorted by their Manhattan distance from the cell (rCenter, cCenter), starting with the closest.
statement: Given the integers row, cols, rCenter, and cCenter, list the coordinates of all cells in a rows x cols matrix, sorted by their Manhattan distance from the cell (rCenter, cCenter), starting with the closest. The Manhattan distance between two cells (r1, c1) and (r2, c2) is calculated as |r1 - r2| + |c1 - c2|.
constraints: Return every cell exactly once ordered by Manhattan distance.
For equal distance, this exercise uses row then column order.
reference_solution:
def cells_by_manhattan_distance(rows, cols, r_center, c_center):
 return sorted(([r,c] for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols)),key=lambda p:(abs(p[0]-r_center)+abs(p[1]-c_center),p[0],p[1]))
hints: Generate all coordinates, then rank them by their distance key.
The key is (absolute row difference + absolute column difference, row, column).
Sort the coordinate list once using that tuple.
Tuple ordering enforces increasing distance and the documented deterministic tie order.
editorial: Tuple ordering enforces increasing distance and the documented deterministic tie order.

tests.explanation: Cells 0,0 and 0,1 have distances zero and one.
The center comes first, followed by tied cells in row-column order.
